etymology: From “papal” (of the pope) and “infallibility” (incapacity of error); the Roman dogma, defined at the First Vatican Council in 1870, that the pope cannot err when defining doctrine ex cathedra.
biblical_def: Papal infallibility is the Roman Catholic dogma, defined at the First Vatican Council in 1870, that the pope, when he speaks ex cathedra—that is, when as supreme pastor he defines a doctrine of faith or morals to be held by the whole church—is preserved from error by divine assistance and his definitions are irreformable of themselves. The dictionary rejects this dogma as contrary to Scripture and as a corruption of the unique authority that belongs to the Word of God alone. Scripture knows but one infallible rule of faith, the inspired Word, and one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus; it nowhere grants an unerring teaching office to any man or succession of men. Peter himself, whom Rome claims as the first pope, was openly rebuked by Paul to his face at Antioch because he was to be blamed—a plain proof that the apostle was not impeccable or unerring in his conduct, still less his supposed successors. The Lord forbade His disciples the very titles and lordship the papacy assumed: “call no man your father upon the earth.” And the noble Bereans were commended for searching the Scriptures daily to test even apostolic preaching, the very opposite of a blind submission to an infallible chair. The dictionary holds that the conscience is bound by Scripture alone (sola Scriptura); councils and bishops may err and have erred; and the claim of an infallible pope, far from securing the truth, has been the instrument of binding the church to errors—indulgences, Marian dogmas, the denial of justification by faith alone—that the Reformation called the church away from on the authority of the Word of God.
webster_summary: The Roman dogma (Vatican I, 1870) that the pope cannot err when defining doctrine ex cathedra; rejected as contrary to Scripture, which knows one infallible rule (the Word) and one Mediator, and records Peter himself rebuked by Paul.

And call no man your father upon the earth: for one is your Father, which is in heaven.

corruption_summary: Papal infallibility is itself the corruption: it usurps for a man the unerring authority Scripture grants to the Word of God alone, and has been used to bind the church to grave error.
corruption_paragraphs: Papal infallibility is not a doctrine the dictionary must guard against drift; it is itself the corruption to be named. Rome claims for the pope, speaking ex cathedra, an immunity from error that Scripture grants to no man. But the Word of God is the only infallible rule of faith, and Christ the only Mediator; the apostles themselves directed the churches to test all teaching by the Scriptures, and Peter—the supposed first pope—was withstood to the face by Paul and blamed. An office that can be rebuked is not an office that cannot err. The dogma exalts a man into the place that belongs to the Word.

The practical fruit of the dogma exposes its falsehood. Far from preserving the church in truth, the claim of infallible papal authority has been the very instrument by which grave errors were imposed and made irreformable—the sale of indulgences, the dogmas of the Immaculate Conception and the bodily Assumption of Mary, the anathemas of Trent against justification by faith alone. The Reformation did not invent a new authority but recalled the church to the old and only one: the Scriptures, which are able to make wise unto salvation, and to which pope, council, and conscience alike must bow. Sola Scriptura is the dictionary's answer to the infallible chair.

etymology: From “Mary” and the Greek latreia (worship, service rendered to God); the excessive veneration of the Virgin Mary that trespasses upon the honour due to God alone.
biblical_def: Mariolatry is the excessive veneration of the Virgin Mary that trespasses upon the worship due to God alone, the corruption by which the mother of the Lord has been exalted in Roman and Eastern practice to a place Scripture never gives her. The dictionary honours Mary truly: she was the favoured one chosen to bear the incarnate Son, blessed among women, a woman of faith and humility whose song magnifies the Lord. But Mary herself confessed her need of a Saviour—“my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour”—and so was a sinner saved by grace like all the redeemed. When a woman cried out blessing on the womb that bore Him, the Lord gently redirected the praise: “Yea rather, blessed are they that hear the word of God, and keep it.” Mary's own last recorded words point men away from herself to her Son: “Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it.” The dictionary names as corruption the accumulated Marian dogmas and devotions of Rome: her Immaculate Conception, her bodily Assumption, her titles as Queen of Heaven, Mediatrix, and Co-Redemptrix, the rosary's repeated prayers addressed to her, and the seeking of her intercession as though she shared the office of the one Mediator. These rob Christ of glory and break the commandment that forbids bowing down to any but God. The dictionary holds the line the Reformation drew: honour Mary as the blessed and believing mother of the Lord, a sinner saved like ourselves, while refusing every prayer, title, and devotion that gives to the creature the worship and mediation belonging to God and to Christ alone.
webster_summary: The excessive veneration of the Virgin Mary trespassing on worship due to God alone; the dictionary honours Mary as the blessed, believing mother of the Lord—herself a sinner saved by grace (Luke 1:47)—while rejecting Rome's Marian dogmas and prayers.

The Lord redirected praise from her womb to obedience to God's word (Luke 11:28).
Rejected: her Immaculate Conception, Assumption, and titles as Mediatrix and Queen of Heaven.

corruption_summary: Mariolatry is itself the corruption: it exalts the creature to a place Scripture never gives her—Mediatrix, Co-Redemptrix, Queen of Heaven—robbing Christ of glory and breaking the command against bowing to any but God.
corruption_paragraphs: Mariolatry is not a doctrine to be guarded against drift but the corruption itself, named plainly. Rome and the East have heaped upon the mother of the Lord titles and devotions that belong to God and to Christ alone: Mediatrix and Co-Redemptrix, Queen of Heaven, the object of prayer and the rosary, credited with an Immaculate Conception and a bodily Assumption Scripture never teaches. The dictionary names these as corruptions of the first and second commandments and as a robbery of the glory of the one Mediator. Mary herself rejoiced in God her Saviour and pointed all to her Son; she neither sought nor received the worship later ages gave her.

The dictionary's correction is not the dishonouring of Mary but the recovery of her true honour. She was indeed blessed among women, the favoured and believing handmaid of the Lord, and the church may rightly call her blessed as she foretold. But she was a sinner saved by grace, as her own song confesses, and the New Testament never directs a prayer to her, never names her a mediator, never bids the church seek her intercession. To honour Mary as Scripture honours her is to magnify the Saviour she magnified; to exalt her as Rome exalts her is to take from Christ the glory He will not share. Whatsoever He saith unto you, do it—her last word remains her best.

etymology: From “Eucharist” (Greek eucharistia, thanksgiving) and “adoration”; the Roman practice of worshipping the consecrated host as the body of Christ, resting on transubstantiation.
biblical_def: Eucharistic adoration is the Roman Catholic practice of worshipping the consecrated host—the bread of the Mass—as the very body of Christ, bowing before it, exposing it in the monstrance, and adoring it as God. It rests upon the dogma of transubstantiation, that at the priest's words the substance of bread and wine is changed into the body and blood of Christ while the appearances remain. The dictionary rejects both the dogma and the adoration as grave corruptions of the Lord's Supper and as idolatry. The Lord instituted the Supper as a memorial and a sign-and-seal: “This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me.” He spoke figuratively, as He did when He called Himself the door and the vine; the bread signifies and seals His body, but is not changed into it. To bow down before bread as God is to worship the creature and to break the second commandment, which forbids the making and adoring of any image or object as the deity. Moreover, God is a Spirit, and they that worship Him must worship Him in spirit and in truth, not in a wafer. The dictionary further holds that the Supper is no repeated sacrifice, for Christ offered one sacrifice for sins for ever and by one offering hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified; the Mass, claiming to re-present that sacrifice, dishonours its finished sufficiency. The Reformed believer feeds upon Christ by faith, receiving Him spiritually present to the soul, and adores Christ enthroned in heaven—never the bread upon the table.
webster_summary: The Roman practice of worshipping the consecrated host as the body of Christ, resting on transubstantiation; rejected as idolatry and a corruption of the Supper, which is a memorial sign (Luke 22:19), not a wafer to be adored or a sacrifice re-offered.
webster_full: EUCHARISTIC ADORATION, noun phrase. The Roman worship of the consecrated host as the body of Christ.

corruption_summary: Eucharistic adoration is itself the corruption: it worships bread as God on the false dogma of transubstantiation, breaking the second commandment and dishonouring the once-for-all sacrifice of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Eucharistic adoration is the corruption to be named, not a doctrine at risk of drift. Resting on transubstantiation, it bids men bow before a wafer and adore it as the living God. The dictionary names this idolatry. The Lord's words “this is my body” are figurative, as when He called Himself the vine and the door; the bread remains bread, a sign and seal of His body given. To worship the creature—here, bread—as the Creator is the very sin the second commandment forbids, and no priestly formula can turn an act of idolatry into worship in spirit and in truth.

The adoration is bound up with the further error of the Mass as a propitiatory sacrifice, re-presenting Christ's offering again and again. But Scripture is emphatic: Christ offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, and by that one offering hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified. To repeat or re-present that sacrifice is to deny its finished sufficiency. The dictionary holds the Reformed doctrine of the Supper: a memorial and a sign-and-seal, in which the believer by faith feeds spiritually upon the Christ who is bodily in heaven, and adores Him there—not in the bread, which he receives in remembrance, but never worships.
roots_summary: From the Greek eucharistia (thanksgiving) and the Latin adoratio (worship); the practice depends on the dogma of transubstantiatio, the supposed change of substance.

pos: noun phrase (the papal monarchy of the Middle Ages)
etymology: From “medieval” (of the Middle Ages) and “papacy”; the office and institution of the Bishop of Rome as it grew, through the medieval centuries, into a monarchy claiming temporal and spiritual supremacy.
biblical_def: The medieval papacy is the office and institution of the Bishop of Rome as it developed through the Middle Ages into a monarchy claiming supremacy over the whole church and over the kings of the earth. From the early honour given the Roman see, the papacy grew—through forged decretals, political alliance, and the decay of rivals—into the towering power of Hildebrand (Gregory VII), Innocent III, and Boniface VIII, who claimed that submission to the Roman pontiff was necessary to salvation for every creature. The dictionary regards this development as the great ecclesiastical corruption the Reformation called the church away from. The Lord forbade His servants the dominion the papacy seized: “the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them… but it shall not be so among you.” Peter charged the elders to feed the flock, not as being lords over God's heritage. Yet the medieval papacy made itself lord, deposing kings, selling indulgences, hoarding a treasury of merit, and binding the conscience by a power that belongs to Christ alone. The Reformers, and the 1689 Confession after them, identified the papal office with the “man of sin” who exalteth himself above all that is called God and sitteth in the temple of God; the Confession names the pope antichrist. The dictionary honours this confessional standard while acknowledging that modern Reformed readers handle the antichrist identification with varied severity. What is not in doubt is the corruption: a monarchy of men usurping the headship of Christ over His church, and obscuring the gospel of free grace under a system of merit, penance, and priestcraft.
webster_summary: The Bishop of Rome's office grown into a medieval monarchy claiming supremacy over church and kings; the great ecclesiastical corruption the Reformation opposed, identified by the Reformers and the 1689 Confession with the “man of sin.”
webster_full: MEDIEVAL PAPACY, noun phrase. The Bishop of Rome's office grown into a monarchy claiming supremacy over church and kings.

corruption_summary: The medieval papacy is itself the corruption: a monarchy of men usurping Christ's headship over His church and obscuring the gospel of grace beneath a system of merit, penance, and priestcraft.
corruption_paragraphs: The medieval papacy is the corruption to be named, not a doctrine to be defended. The Bishop of Rome, claiming a supremacy Scripture never granted, made himself the monarch of the church and arbiter of kings, deposing rulers, claiming both swords, and asserting that submission to him was necessary for salvation. The Lord had expressly forbidden such lordship among His servants, and Peter—whom Rome claims as the first pope—charged the elders not to lord it over God's heritage. The papal monarchy usurped the sole headship of Christ over His church, and the dictionary names it the great ecclesiastical corruption from which the Reformation was deliverance.

The corruption was doctrinal as well as institutional. Bound up with the papal claims were the sale of indulgences, the treasury of merit, the multiplication of penances, and a priestcraft that interposed itself between the sinner and his Saviour, obscuring the gospel of justification by faith alone. The Reformers, reading 2 Thessalonians 2 and Revelation 17, identified the papal office with the man of sin who exalts himself in the temple of God, and the 1689 London Baptist Confession names the pope that antichrist. The dictionary honours this confessional standard, while noting that modern Reformed readers vary in the severity with which they press the identification; the substance, however, stands—the medieval papacy darkened the gospel and usurped the crown of Christ.

pos: proper noun (a missionary; first Archbishop of Canterbury)
etymology: Named for Augustine (Latin Augustinus); the Benedictine monk sent by Gregory the Great to England in A.D. 597, not to be confused with Augustine of Hippo.
biblical_def: Augustine of Canterbury (died c. 604) was the Benedictine prior sent by Gregory the Great from Rome to the Anglo-Saxons of England in A.D. 597, becoming the first Archbishop of Canterbury and the leader of the mission that planted the Roman form of Christianity among the English. He is to be carefully distinguished from the far greater Augustine of Hippo. The dictionary honours what is honourable in his work: he obeyed the missionary impulse of the Great Commission—“Go ye therefore, and teach all nations”—and carried the name of Christ to a heathen people, baptizing King Ethelbert of Kent and many of his subjects, so that the gospel, however mixed, reached a pagan land. The labour of carrying glad tidings to those who had not heard is in itself a beautiful thing, for how shall they believe without a preacher. Yet the dictionary does not idealize him. The Christianity he planted was the developing Roman religion, with its sacramentalism, its veneration of relics and saints, and its submission to the papal see; and his dealings with the older Celtic British church were marked by a haughty insistence on Roman customs (the dating of Easter, the form of baptism, submission to himself) that bred division rather than unity. The dictionary applies its rule for non-Reformed figures: it honours the genuine missionary zeal that brought Christ's name to the English, while naming the Roman errors he carried with it. The conversion of England was a real mercy of God; the Roman dress in which it came was a corruption later generations, and at last the English Reformation, would have to strip away.
webster_summary: The Benedictine monk sent by Gregory the Great to England in 597, first Archbishop of Canterbury (not Augustine of Hippo); honoured for the missionary zeal that brought Christ's name to the English, while the Roman errors he planted are named.

corruption_summary: Augustine of Canterbury carried the developing Roman religion—sacramentalism, relics, submission to the papal see—to England, and his haughty dealings with the older British church bred division, not unity.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary honours the genuine good in Augustine of Canterbury's mission. He obeyed the Great Commission, leaving Rome at Gregory's sending to carry the gospel to a heathen people, and under his preaching King Ethelbert and many of the men of Kent were baptized. That the name of Christ reached the Anglo-Saxons through his labour is a mercy of God, for how beautiful are the feet of them that bring glad tidings, and how shall a people believe without a preacher sent to them. The missionary impulse itself is to be commended wherever it is found.

Yet the dictionary will not idealize the mission or its fruit. The Christianity Augustine planted was the developing Roman religion, freighted with the sacramentalism, the veneration of relics and saints, and the submission to the papal see that the Reformation would later have to call the church away from. His dealings with the older Celtic British Christians, who had kept the faith in Britain long before him, were marked by a proud insistence on Roman usages and on submission to himself, breeding division rather than the unity of the Spirit. The dictionary applies its standing rule: honour the missionary zeal, name the Roman errors—the conversion of England was a real work of God, in a Roman dress that needed at last to be stripped away.

pos: noun phrase (a form of liturgical music)
etymology: Named for Gregory the Great, to whom its codification was traditionally ascribed; the unaccompanied plainsong (monophonic chant) of the medieval Western church.
biblical_def: Gregorian chant is the unaccompanied, single-melody plainsong of the medieval Western church, traditionally ascribed to the ordering of Gregory the Great, sung in Latin for the Mass and the daily offices. It is monophonic—one unharmonized line—flowing in free rhythm to the words of the psalms and liturgy, and it shaped the worship music of Western Christendom for a thousand years. The dictionary treats it as a matter of the history and principles of worship. Much in the chant tradition reflects a true instinct: the words of Scripture, especially the Psalms, set to music that serves the text rather than overwhelming it, sung in reverence and order, lifting the heart to God. Scripture commands the singing of psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, making melody in the heart to the Lord, and the chant at its best embodies the seriousness and word-centredness that worship ought to have. Yet the dictionary, holding the regulative principle of worship, raises its cautions. The chant was bound to a Latin liturgy the people could not understand, contrary to the apostolic rule that worship be intelligible, that the church may say Amen; it served the corrupt Mass and its sacrifice; and it was the music of a clerical performance more than the song of the congregation. The dictionary's judgment is measured: it honours the reverence, the textual fidelity, and the beauty of the chant tradition, and the church may learn from its seriousness; but it holds that worship song must be in the language of the people, must serve sound doctrine, and must be the praise of the whole congregation, not a priestly art performed over them.
webster_summary: The unaccompanied Latin plainsong of the medieval Western church, ascribed to Gregory the Great; honoured for its reverence and fidelity to the psalm-text, yet weighed by the regulative principle—worship must be intelligible and congregational, not clerical performance.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the apostolic shape of sung worship. The dictionary gladly honours much in the chant tradition—its reverence, its free and unhurried setting of the psalm-text, its seriousness, its refusal to let melody trample the words. In an age of trivial and self-centred worship music, the chant's word-centred gravity is a rebuke worth hearing, and the church may learn from it. The instinct to sing the Scriptures, especially the Psalms, with melody serving the text is thoroughly biblical.

Yet the dictionary, holding the regulative principle, raises three cautions without manufacturing grievance. The chant was bound to a Latin liturgy the people could not understand, against the apostle's clear rule that worship be intelligible, that the unlearned may say Amen (1 Corinthians 14:16); it served the Mass with its false sacrifice; and it became increasingly the performance of clergy and choir over a silent congregation, rather than the praise of the whole people of God. The dictionary's measured judgment: honour the reverence and fidelity of the chant, learn from its seriousness, but hold that the song of the church must be in the language of the people, must serve sound doctrine, and must rise from the whole congregation's heart to the Lord.

pos: proper noun (a work of Gregory the Great)
etymology: From the Latin Liber Regulae Pastoralis (“Book of the Pastoral Rule”), Gregory the Great's treatise (c. 591) on the office and care of the pastor.
biblical_def: The Pastoral Rule (Latin Liber Regulae Pastoralis) is the treatise on the pastoral office written by Gregory the Great about A.D. 591, one of the most influential handbooks on the care of souls in the history of the church. In it Gregory sets forth who is fit to undertake the pastoral charge, how the pastor ought to live, how he should teach—adapting his admonition to the varied conditions of his hearers—and how he must guard against pride by daily self-examination. The dictionary treats it as a matter of the doctrine of the ministry. Much in the Pastoral Rule reflects the biblical charge to shepherds: Peter bids the elders feed the flock of God, taking the oversight not by constraint nor for filthy lucre but willingly; Paul charges the Ephesian elders to feed the church of God which He purchased with His own blood; Ezekiel thunders against shepherds who feed themselves and not the flock; and the office of overseer is called a good work to be desired. Gregory's insistence that the shepherd care for souls, suit his teaching to each, and watch his own heart is sound and edifying, and the work has profited faithful pastors of every age, the Reformers included. Yet the dictionary does not receive it uncritically. It bears the marks of its age and author: a developing sacerdotalism that views the pastor increasingly as a sacrificing priest, an asceticism shaped by the monastic ideal, and assumptions tied to the rising Roman hierarchy. The dictionary applies its rule: honour the genuine pastoral wisdom and the high view of the care of souls, while reading it through the corrective of Scripture and the recovered doctrine of the pastor as preacher and shepherd, not sacrificing priest.
webster_summary: Gregory the Great's treatise (c. 591) on the pastoral office and the care of souls; honoured for its biblical wisdom on shepherding (1 Peter 5:2; Acts 20:28), yet read critically for its developing sacerdotalism and monastic assumptions.

Yet it bears a developing sacerdotalism and monastic asceticism, to be read through Scripture.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the high biblical view of the care of souls. The Pastoral Rule's great worth is its seriousness about the pastoral office: that none should lightly undertake it, that the shepherd must live what he preaches, that he should suit his admonition to the varied conditions of his people, and that he must daily guard his heart against the pride that the office breeds. All this echoes Peter's charge to feed the flock willingly and Paul's to feed the church God purchased with His own blood. The dictionary honours the work as a genuine treasure of pastoral wisdom from which faithful ministers of every age have profited.

Yet the dictionary reads it critically, as it reads all the fathers. The Rule bears the marks of its author and age: a developing sacerdotalism that views the pastor increasingly as a priest offering sacrifice rather than a shepherd preaching the word, an asceticism shaped by the monastic ideal, and assumptions bound up with the rising Roman hierarchy. The dictionary applies its standing rule for non-Reformed sources—honour what is honourable, name the error. Read through the corrective of Scripture and the recovered Reformation doctrine of the minister as preacher and shepherd of souls, the Pastoral Rule remains a profitable guide; received uncritically, it carries the seeds of the priestcraft the Reformation had to undo.

pos: proper noun (a treatise of Martin Bucer)
etymology: Latin, “On the Kingdom of Christ”; the treatise written by the Reformer Martin Bucer in 1550 for the young King Edward VI of England, on the reform of church and commonwealth under Christ's kingship.
biblical_def: De Regno Christi (“On the Kingdom of Christ”) is the major treatise of the Strasbourg Reformer Martin Bucer, written in 1550 during his English exile and presented to the young King Edward VI, setting forth a comprehensive program for the reform of both church and commonwealth under the kingship of Christ. Bucer argued that Christ is King over all of life, and that a Christian realm should order its worship, its church discipline, its laws, its care of the poor, its marriage and education, in conformity to the law and gospel of God. The dictionary treats the work as a witness to the Reformed doctrine of the kingship of Christ. Its great truth is biblical: the Father has set His King upon His holy hill, declared that He must reign till He hath put all enemies under His feet, and bidden His people pray, “Thy kingdom come, thy will be done in earth.” Christ's lordship is not confined to a private spiritual sphere but extends over every realm of human life. The dictionary honours Bucer's vision against the modern privatizing of faith and the Radical Two-Kingdoms error that would shut Christ out of the public square. Yet it also marks the work's limitations and the cautions of later Reformed reflection: Bucer's program leaned heavily on the godly magistrate to enforce reformation, a Constantinian and theocratic confidence that the Baptist tradition, with its insistence on liberty of conscience and the spiritual nature of Christ's kingdom, would temper. The dictionary thus commends the central truth—the universal kingship of Christ—while reading the magistrate's role through the corrective of the 1689 Confession's fuller doctrine of conscience and the church's spiritual power.
webster_summary: Martin Bucer's 1550 treatise for Edward VI on the reform of church and commonwealth under Christ's kingship; honoured for the truth of Christ's universal lordship (Psalm 2:6; 1 Corinthians 15:25), tempered by the Baptist doctrine of conscience and the spiritual kingdom.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the universal kingship of Christ. Bucer's great and biblical truth is that Christ reigns as King over all of life—over worship, law, family, education, the care of the poor—and that no realm of human existence lies outside His lordship. The Father has set His King on Zion, and He must reign till every enemy is under His feet. The dictionary honours this against the modern privatizing of faith and especially against the Radical Two-Kingdoms error, which would confine Christ's rule to an inner spiritual sphere and shut Him out of public life.

Yet the dictionary marks the limitations of Bucer's program and the cautions of later Reformed reflection, without disparaging the man or the truth he served. Bucer leaned heavily on the godly magistrate to compel reformation by the sword of the state—a Constantinian and theocratic confidence shared by much of the magisterial Reformation. The Baptist tradition, and the 1689 Confession after it, while affirming Christ's universal kingship, tempered this with a fuller doctrine of liberty of conscience and the spiritual nature of Christ's kingdom, which advances by the Word and Spirit, not by the magistrate's coercion. The dictionary commends the kingship of Christ that De Regno Christi proclaims, while reading the magistrate's role through that corrective.

etymology: Latin Constantius; the son of Constantine the Great who reigned A.D. 337-361 and used imperial power to advance Arianism against Nicene orthodoxy.
biblical_def: Constantius II (reigned A.D. 337-361) was a son of Constantine the Great and emperor of the Eastern and later the whole Roman Empire, remembered in church history as the ruler who threw the weight of the imperial throne behind Arianism, the heresy that denied the full deity of the Son of God. Where his father had presided over the Council of Nicaea that confessed the Son to be of one substance with the Father, Constantius favoured the Arian and semi-Arian parties, pressured councils to overturn Nicene orthodoxy, and persecuted its defenders—above all Athanasius of Alexandria, whom he drove repeatedly into exile. It was of this era that Jerome wrote, “The whole world groaned and was astonished to find itself Arian.” The dictionary marks Constantius II as a sobering case of the union of political power with doctrinal error. He illustrates the danger of the state lording it over the church's faith, and the truth that the majority and the throne are no measure of orthodoxy: when emperors and councils leaned toward Arianism, the truth was upheld by a persecuted few, chiefly Athanasius—Athanasius contra mundum, Athanasius against the world. He also embodies the apostle's warning of men who will not endure sound doctrine, and the Arian sin of changing the truth of God into a lie and serving the creature more than the Creator, for to deny the Son's full deity is to worship a creature. The dictionary holds the lesson: in Christ dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily; the faith stands on the Word of God, not on the favour of princes, in whom there is no help; and God preserves His truth through faithful witnesses even when the powers of the age conspire against it.
webster_summary: The son of Constantine (reigned 337-361) who used imperial power to advance Arianism and persecute Athanasius; a case of political power wedded to doctrinal error, showing that throne and majority are no measure of orthodoxy.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; it stands as a warning against the state coercing the church's faith and against measuring orthodoxy by the throne or the majority.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the truth of God does not stand or fall with the favour of princes or the verdict of the majority. Constantius II marshalled the whole weight of the imperial throne behind Arianism, bent councils to his will, and drove the defenders of Nicene orthodoxy into exile; for a season it seemed the church had become Arian. Yet the truth was preserved—not by the emperor, not by the councils he pressured, but by a persecuted remnant, chiefly Athanasius, who stood against the world. The lesson is perennial: orthodoxy is measured by the Word of God, not by the powers of the age.

Constantius also exposes the gravity of the Arian heresy he favoured. To deny the full deity of the Son is, in the apostle's terms, to change the truth of God into a lie and to worship and serve the creature more than the Creator; for if Christ is less than fully God, then Christian worship of Him is creature-worship. But in Him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily. The dictionary marks Constantius II as a sober witness against the union of political coercion with doctrinal error, and as an encouragement that God preserves His truth through faithful witnesses—put not your trust in princes, in whom there is no help, but in the LORD who keepeth truth for ever.

etymology: Greek Pantokrator, “ruler of all, Almighty,” from pas (all) and krateo (to rule, to hold power); the New Testament title of God and of Christ, rendered “Almighty” in the Authorized Version.
biblical_def: Pantokrator is the Greek title meaning “ruler of all” or “Almighty,” used in the New Testament of God and of the exalted Christ, and rendered “Almighty” or “omnipotent” in the Authorized Version. It renders the Hebrew names of God's power—El Shaddai, God Almighty, and LORD of hosts—and proclaims that God holds all things in His hand and rules over all. The risen Christ declares, “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending, saith the Lord, which is, and which was, and which is to come, the Almighty”; and the multitude of heaven cries, “Alleluia: for the Lord God omnipotent reigneth.” The title confesses the omnipotence and absolute sovereignty of God: that He upholds all things by the word of His power, that nothing is too hard for Him, and that He doeth according to His will in the army of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth. The dictionary holds Pantokrator as a precious confession of the deity and almighty rule of both the Father and the Son, a bulwark against every theology that diminishes the power of God—against Open Theism, which denies His exhaustive knowledge and sovereign control, and against process theology, which makes Him a finite, struggling deity. The God of Scripture is the Pantokrator, the Almighty who reigns. The dictionary also notes, without manufacturing grievance, the proper caution attending the famous Eastern icon-type “Christ Pantokrator”: the title is glorious and biblical, but the practice of venerating images of Christ falls under the dictionary's rejection of icon-worship per the second commandment. The word itself is to be cherished; the Almighty reigns, and to Him belongs all worship.
webster_summary: The Greek title “Almighty, ruler of all,” used of God and the exalted Christ (Revelation 1:8; 19:6); a confession of divine omnipotence and sovereignty, a bulwark against Open Theism and process theology that diminish God's power.

corruption_summary: The title is corrupted by Open Theism and process theology, which deny God's exhaustive knowledge and omnipotence; the Eastern icon “Christ Pantokrator” pairs a glorious title with image-veneration the dictionary rejects.
corruption_paragraphs: The chief corruption touching Pantokrator is doctrinal: the modern theologies that deny the very omnipotence the title confesses. Open Theism (Pinnock, Boyd, Sanders) holds that God does not exhaustively foreknow or sovereignly control the future, making the Almighty a God who waits and guesses; process theology makes Him finite, changing, and struggling alongside the world rather than ruling over it. The dictionary names both as departures from the God of Scripture and from every historic confession. The Pantokrator upholds all things by the word of His power, does according to His will in heaven and earth, and reigns—the title itself rebukes every diminished deity.

A second and lesser caution attends the famous Eastern icon-type called “Christ Pantokrator,” the image of Christ as Almighty ruler that adorns the domes of Orthodox churches. The dictionary cherishes the title as glorious and biblical while rejecting, per the second commandment, the veneration of images of Christ that the icon tradition entails. This is no manufactured grievance but the consistent application of the Reformed doctrine of worship: God is to be worshipped in spirit and in truth, not through images. The word Pantokrator is to be loved and confessed; the Almighty reigns, the Lord God omnipotent, and to Him alone—not to His image—belongs all worship.
